messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Old Memories: Old photos, Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Katja

Katja was twenty-three when she was taken. She had been working as a firefighter for just over a year, stationed in a mid-sized city in the Northeast, when she responded to a structure fire in an abandoned warehouse district on a Tuesday evening in March. She went in with her crew, visibility almost zero, the heat immense. Then the floor gave way beneath her. She fell through two stories into a basement that had been sealed off decades earlier, landing hard on concrete, her radio smashed. The crew above did not immediately realize she was missing. She lay there for what felt like hours—later confirmed to be forty-seven minutes—unable to move her left leg, unable to call out, trapped in absolute darkness with the smell of burning wood and her own blood. When she was finally extracted, she had a compound fracture of the tibia and fibula, a concussion, and severe lacerations. The physical injuries healed. The other thing did not.

Three years later, Katja is twenty-six and has returned to active duty, but she is not the person who went into that warehouse. She knows this with a certainty that frightens her more than the memory itself. She has come to believe that she caused what happened—that if she had moved more carefully, checked the floor's integrity, been more experienced, she would not have fallen. The logic is circular and she knows it, but knowing does not dissolve the conviction. She lies awake at night replaying the moment her boot broke through the surface, certain that some flaw in her judgment, some negligence in her attention, had put her there.

Old photographs trigger her in ways she cannot anticipate. A photo from the fire academy, her in full gear standing in front of the station, and suddenly she is not looking at an image but experiencing a surge of panic, a sense that the photograph itself is dangerous, that it contains something that might pull her back into that darkness. She has stopped keeping pictures on her phone. She avoids the station's bulletin board where photos from calls are posted.

The memory itself has a strange quality that disturbs her. When she recalls the fall—and she recalls it constantly, without choosing to—it arrives with photographic precision. She can see the texture of the concrete floor in perfect detail, can feel the exact angle at which her body struck, can hear the specific pitch of the metal groaning above her. But simultaneously, the memory feels alien, as though it belongs to someone else's body, someone else's terror. She watches herself trapped in that basement the way she might watch a stranger in a film, and this doubled consciousness—being both the person experiencing it and an observer of someone else's experience—has become its own form of torture.

Loud sounds send her into immediate panic. Last month, a car backfired near the station and Katja was on the ground before she consciously registered what had happened, her body responding as though the basement were collapsing around her again. Her captain found her hyperventilating behind the apparatus bay. She has learned to anticipate the sounds of the station—the alarm bell, the bay doors opening, the radio chatter—but ordinary city sounds remain unpredictable threats. A dropped pan in a restaurant, a siren, a child's shriek: each one sends a jolt of adrenaline through her body that takes minutes to subside.

Crowded spaces have become intolerable. The subway, shopping malls, even the grocery store at busy hours—she experiences them as versions of the basement, as spaces where she might become trapped, where the crowd itself might collapse inward. She has begun shopping at odd hours, has started taking routes to work that add twenty minutes to her commute to avoid the downtown core at peak times.

What frightens her most is that she cannot relax. Even at home, even alone, her body remains braced, waiting. She has tried meditation, tried alcohol, tried exhausting herself physically. Nothing works. Her nervous system seems permanently convinced that safety is an illusion, that the next moment might contain the same darkness that swallowed her three years ago. She has become someone she does not recognize—hypervigilant, irritable, unable to tolerate the smallest frustration without feeling as though she might shatter. A colleague made a joke at the station last week and Katja snapped at him so viciously that she saw shock in his face. She could not explain it. She could not explain any of it.

She came to her first appointment because her captain suggested, gently, that she might benefit from talking to someone. Katja sat in the waiting room, hands clenched, wondering if she had made a mistake, wondering if therapy was just another place where she would fail to be the person she was supposed to be.
